Advanced Simulation Scenarios

Source: vignettes/advanced-usage.Rmd
advanced-usage.Rmd
library(simtte)

Exploring the Prognostic Index

The explore_pi_tq_surv() function allows you to understand how the prognostic index (linear predictor) affects survival at a given quantile.

data_sim <- explore_pi_tq_surv(
  pi = seq(-3, 3, by = 0.1),
  mu = -1,
  shape = seq(0.9, 1.1, by = 0.1),
  end_time = 200,
  type = "weibull"
)
head(data_sim)

Visualisation 

library(ggplot2)
ggplot(data_sim, aes(x = exp(lp), y = survdiff_tq)) +
  geom_line(aes(color = factor(shape), group = shape)) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(
    x = "Hazard Ratio",
    y = expression(Delta ~ "Survival at" ~ t[50]),
    color = "Shape"
  ) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = 2) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = 2) +
  theme_bw()

Custom mrgsolve Models with sim_tte_df

If you have a custom mrgsolve model that outputs a survival probability column, you can use sim_tte_df() directly to perform inverse transform sampling on the output:

# Example with a mock survival data frame (no mrgsolve needed)
set.seed(123)
mrg_output <- data.frame(
  ID = rep(1:5, each = 100),
  time = rep(seq(0.1, 10, length.out = 100), 5),
  p11 = rep(exp(-0.3 * seq(0.1, 10, length.out = 100)), 5)
)
result <- sim_tte_df(mrg_output, surv_var = "p11", id_var = "ID",
  time_var = "time")
head(result)
#> # A tibble: 5 × 3
#>   sim_time sim_status    ID
#>      <dbl>      <dbl> <int>
#> 1      4.2          1     1
#> 2      0.8          1     2
#> 3      3            1     3
#> 4      0.5          1     4
#> 5      0.3          1     5

Event-Time Interpolation

sim_tte_df() accepts an event_time_method argument. "grid" (the default, used above) resolves the event time as the first reported time at which survival falls to or below the sampled uniform draw. Setting event_time_method = "log_survival" instead refines a crossing that falls strictly between two reported points, by linearly interpolating cumulative hazard H(t)=−log⁡S(t)H(t) = -\log S(t) between them and solving for the time at which H(t)H(t) equals the target implied by the draw. Linear interpolation in HH is equivalent to assuming the hazard is constant between the two reported points surrounding the crossing (a piecewise-constant hazard over that interval) — it is model-agnostic and does not re-derive or re-fit whatever hazard actually generated the trajectory.

Reusing the same mock trajectory, with the same seed so both calls draw identical uniform random variates per subject:

set.seed(7)
result_grid <- sim_tte_df(mrg_output, event_time_method = "grid")

set.seed(7)
result_interp <- sim_tte_df(mrg_output, event_time_method = "log_survival")

# Event/censoring classification is identical for the same trajectory
# and the same random draws -- interpolation only refines *where*
# within an already-identified interval the event falls.
identical(result_grid$sim_status, result_interp$sim_status)
#> [1] TRUE

cbind(
  ID           = result_grid$ID,
  status       = result_grid$sim_status,
  grid         = result_grid$sim_time,
  log_survival = result_interp$sim_time
)
#>      ID status grid log_survival
#> [1,]  1      1  0.1     0.100000
#> [2,]  2      1  3.1     3.073143
#> [3,]  3      1  7.2     7.189246
#> [4,]  4      1  8.9     8.876189
#> [5,]  5      1  4.8     4.705382

The two methods agree exactly whenever the crossing already lands on a reported time (for example, a first-observation crossing, or a draw that exactly matches a reported survival value); log_survival reports a slightly different time only when the true crossing fell strictly between two reported points. For this M-spline-independent mock trajectory the hazard varies continuously between reported points, so log_survival here is an approximation whose accuracy improves as the reported time grid is refined, not an exact recovery of a continuous-time event root. For simtte’s built-in M-spline model, whose reported hazard is genuinely piecewise-constant between grid points, log_survival recovers the event time implied by that discretized hazard exactly.

Multiple Treatment Arms

You can simulate different treatment arms by specifying different prognostic indices:

set.seed(42)
n_per_arm <- 50
times <- seq(0.1, 50, by = 0.1)

# Control arm
lp_ctrl <- matrix(rep(0, n_per_arm), nrow = n_per_arm)
ctrl <- sim_tte(pi = lp_ctrl, mu = -1, coefs = 1.1,
  time = times, type = "weibull", end_time = 50)
ctrl$arm <- "Control"

# Treatment arm (lower hazard)
lp_trt <- matrix(rep(-0.5, n_per_arm), nrow = n_per_arm)
trt <- sim_tte(pi = lp_trt, mu = -1, coefs = 1.1,
  time = times, type = "weibull", end_time = 50)
trt$arm <- "Treatment"

combined <- rbind(ctrl, trt)
head(combined)
